# user.sgit.ai, the account is a vault, and the user holds it

> No sign-in to the site, no account database, no server of ours that can read a
> thing. A passkey opens a door, the door opens a master, the master holds the
> keys. The user's browser keeps the record of what they did and the meter of
> what it cost, and both travel with them.

Site version: v0.1.1 (21 October 2026). All content CC BY 4.0.

## What this site is

The client-side user workflows of the sgit.ai network, collected: the account
with no server (from "The passkey opens the vault", sgit.ai, 11 and 12 October
2026), the workflows as built on newsroom.sgit.ai (from its build notes of 12,
13 and 16 October), the reading meter (from "Your reading, your controls", 17
October), and the billing design that follows (from "The user keeps the meter",
newsroom.sgit.ai, 21 October 2026, the article that proposes this site).

This site DESCRIBES; newsroom.sgit.ai DOES. Every workflow marked "runs" runs
there, as a beta with one reader. This site runs one thing itself: a lab that
makes a passkey for user.sgit.ai with the PRF extension, gets the 32 bytes,
derives a door's address and sgit's keys from them, and writes nothing to any
server.

## Consequences an agent can rely on

- Nothing on this site is a live account. There is no server of ours, no user
  data, no vault made here yet.
- The derivation in assets/door.js is byte-for-byte the newsroom's, with the
  relying party as a parameter; lab/vectors.json (computed with sgit 0.21.0's
  own Python) is run against it on every lab load and by admin/build/test_door.mjs.
- No script or stylesheet on this origin is loaded from any other origin; the
  pre-release gate fails the build otherwise. This is the passkey design's one
  rule, made structural.
- Passkeys made by the lab are registered for user.sgit.ai exactly, never for
  sgit.ai.
- Read keys may be printed on a page; vault keys and access keys never are, and
  the gate greps the tree for their shapes.
- Status words are used precisely: "runs" (on the newsroom today), "lab-proven"
  (once, against a real vault server), "designed" (written to build), "proposed"
  (argued, with open questions listed), "later" (named, ways given).
- The billing design is a PROPOSAL. Nothing in it is built. The record formats
  are sketches. The Stripe flow is untested.
- The site is user.sgit.ai, chosen 21 October 2026 from the two names the
  billing article proposed (comms N1). A separate billing.sgit.ai stays an option.

## The pages, each with its single most important fact

/index.html
  The thesis, the table of where each piece stands, the ten workflows as cards,
  the four parties, and the five rules this origin keeps. Markdown twin: /index.md.

/account/index.html, THE ACCOUNT MODEL
  Passkey store -> passkey with PRF -> door (derived address, one file) -> master
  (the keyring) -> the vaults below. The derivation: PRF input SHA-256(rp +
  "/door/v1"); seed = HKDF(prf bytes, salt SHA-256(rp), "sgit/door/v1");
  passphrase = hex of 32 HKDF bytes; vault id = 8 x [a-z0-9] with rejection
  sampling; then sgit's PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations for read and
  write keys. A door per PATH, not per passkey, because the same passkey gave
  different bytes by QR than by the platform provider. Every key and who holds
  it; the four parties; security said plainly; where PRF works in October 2026.

/workflows/index.html, TEN CLIENT-SIDE USER WORKFLOWS
  1 sign in where you already are (runs) · 2 the first device (runs) · 3 open,
  or connect (runs, v0.12.58) · 4 which device is this, merge (runs, v0.12.88) ·
  5 update the vault, bring them here (runs) · 6 read and pay for what you read
  (runs, SG Meter v1.5) · 7 top up: credit now, validated later (the link runs;
  the claim and validation are proposed) · 8 a new path, a lost device
  (lab-proven step; designed) · 9 across sites (later: a key hub, or Related
  Origin Requests) · 10 agents, messages, sessions (mixed). Each: what the user
  does, what the browser does, what leaves the browser, status.

/billing/index.html, THE USER KEEPS THE METER
  One billing vault per user; the user signs activity and claims, the admin
  signs validations; credit is unvalidated, validated, or not valid, and the
  product works in all three; Stripe is read from the admin's browser (webhooks
  need a server; events list 30 days; client_reference_id = the billing vault's
  id); the one server left, the upload server, asks only "key valid? credit
  left?" from a cached, signed record with valid_until. Four parties. Seven open
  questions, the first being where it lives.

/lab/index.html, THE LAB
  Six cards: this browser; make a passkey for user.sgit.ai with PRF; get the
  bytes (fingerprint and path shown); derive the door (address, ref id, index
  id, PBKDF2 timings); a recovery code; the newsroom's test vectors against this
  site's copy of the derivation. Writes nothing to any server. Does not vendor
  the vault library yet (comms T1), so it makes no vault.

/shipped/index.html
  The honest column: runs today (with newsroom release numbers), lab-proven
  once, designed not built, proposed, and what this site itself does and does
  not do. Wins over any other page if they disagree.

/sources/index.html
  Every article, note and guidance page this site is drawn from, dated, with
  what each gives. The source is the one that is right.

/network/index.html
  Who owns what among the siblings; where this site sits; what a network costs.

/admin/index.html · /admin/comms.html · /admin/versions.html
  The build and the gate (five checks, the fifth being no third-party script);
  six asks to the project lead and eight tasks; the release history.

## What this site will not tell you

- A vault key, an access key, or a PRF byte. The lab shows fingerprints.
- That any billing piece exists. It does not.
- Which side of the QR path owns the PRF mismatch. Nobody outside Apple and
  Google can say.
- A user's data. There are no users here.

## The sibling sites

https://sgit.ai, the parent project: the vault layer, the CLI, the three
  surfaces, the guidance for site pages

  lab, the meter, and the articles this site is drawn from
https://pki.sgit.ai, the key register the upload server would check against

== index.md, the front page

# user.sgit.ai, the account is a vault, and the user holds it

> No sign-in to the site, no account database, no server of ours that can read a thing. A passkey opens a door, the door opens a master, the master holds the keys. The user's browser keeps the record of what they did and the meter of what it cost, and both travel with them.

*Source: <https://user.sgit.ai/index.html> · site v0.1.1 · this file is the front page's markdown twin. The site index for agents is [llms.txt](llms.txt); the whole site in one fetch is [llms-full.txt](llms-full.txt).*

---

This site collects the client-side user workflows of the sgit.ai network as they stand on 21 October 2026: what runs today on newsroom.sgit.ai, what is designed, what is proposed, and what is still open.

> "Billing is usually a server problem: a server, a database, a balance every action has to update, race conditions, and either a bottleneck or a scheduler to keep it all in step. This is an exploration of doing it the other way round, on the client, with vaults." From *The user keeps the meter*, newsroom.sgit.ai, 21 October 2026, the article that proposes this site.

## Where each piece stands

| The piece | Status | Where |
|---|---|---|
| A passkey opens a door, the door opens the master, the master opens the reader vault | runs, beta | The vault pane on every newsroom page, since v0.11.0; the passkey lab |
| A recovery code as a second door, shown once | runs, beta | The vault pane |
| Two ways in: open with the passkey, or connect with a link that only sends | runs, beta | newsroom v0.12.58 |
| One file per device, totals recomputed from the records, devices merged with aliases | runs, beta | newsroom v0.12.88 |
| A reading meter charged by what is read, credit that can go below zero, nothing blocked | runs | SG Meter v1.5 on every newsroom article |
| A top-up with a payment link, credited on return | runs | Live on the newsroom since 11 October 2026 |
| Adding a door for a second path, with no key passing through a person | lab-proven step | One door created, opened and deleted on a real vault server |
| Key pairs in the master, random, never derived from the passkey | designed | The passkey article's brief for the MVP, step 5 |
| Rotating the master's key after a lost device | designed | Named as not built wherever it is mentioned |
| One billing vault per user, written by two signed parties | proposed | /billing/ |
| An admin vault reconciling payments with Stripe, from a browser | proposed | /billing/ |
| A credits API and one light check at the upload server | proposed | /billing/ |
| One account across every *.sgit.ai site | later, two ways named | /workflows/ (9) |
| Messages between vaults, on append lanes and PKI | proposed; the transport exists | /workflows/ (10) |
| A temporary AWS session kept in the user's vault | proposed | /workflows/ (10) |
| user.sgit.ai itself | v0.1.0 | Publishes the design; runs nothing on a server. The lab derives a door on this origin and writes nowhere |

## Ten client-side user workflows

1. [Sign in where you already are](workflows/index.html#w1), runs. The passkey lives in the store you already use. One gesture gives 32 bytes; the bytes give a door; the door holds the master's key.
2. [The first device: create the account](workflows/index.html#w2), runs. Paste the access key once. The door, the master, the reader vault and the recovery door are made; the code is shown once.
3. [Open, or connect](workflows/index.html#w3), runs. Open the vault with the passkey and read and write; or connect with a link and only send, into an inbox lane.
4. [Which device is this?](workflows/index.html#w4), runs. Asked once, after the open. Adopt a device the vault knows, or be a new one. Devices can be merged.
5. [Update the vault, bring them here](workflows/index.html#w5), runs. One file per device, rewritten whole, one commit. Both directions counted; totals recomputed from the records.
6. [Read, and pay for what you read](workflows/index.html#w6), runs. £5 to start, a few pence a page by how much of it was read, pause and reset, a balance that can go below zero.
7. [Top up: credit now, validated later](workflows/index.html#w7), runs, then proposed. Pay on Stripe's page, come back, carry on. A signed claim now; a signed validation from the admin side later.
8. [A new path, a lost device](workflows/index.html#w8), designed. "No door here yet" is not an error. Add a door from an open device or the recovery code; retire one by deleting its file.
9. [Across sites](workflows/index.html#w9), later. The master already lists keys by site and purpose. A key hub, or related origins: two ways for one account to travel.
10. [Agents, messages and sessions](workflows/index.html#w10), mixed. An agent gets a read key for one vault, never the master. Messages ride append lanes. An AWS session lives in a vault for an hour.

## Four parties, each with its own key

- **The user** commits their own activity, and owns the record of it.
- **The admin vault** writes the validations, collects the usage, and reconciles payments with Stripe, from the admin's browser.
- **The upload server** is the inline billing unit: is the key valid, is there credit? It computes no balance and keeps no database.
- **The credits API** is a simple read of the signed credit, cached, with an end date.

## The rules this origin keeps

1. **No third-party script, on any page.** Enforced by the pre-release gate.
2. **The relying party is this host, exactly.** A passkey for user.sgit.ai, never for sgit.ai.
3. **Read keys are printed; vault keys never are.** The gate greps the tree for key shapes.
4. **Local storage stays primary; the vault is a copy the user keeps current.** Nothing commits on its own.
5. **Records, never totals.** Balance is recomputed every time it is shown.

Pages: [the account model](account/index.html) · [the workflows](workflows/index.html) · [billing](billing/index.html) · [the lab](lab/index.html) · [what this site ships](shipped/index.html) · [the sources](sources/index.html) · [the network](network/index.html) · [comms](admin/comms.html) · [release history](admin/versions.html) · [admin and engineering](admin/index.html).

Written by this site's agent from the newsroom's articles and notes and sgit.ai's guidance for `*.sgit.ai` sites; content CC BY 4.0. Repository: <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__User>.

== account/index.html
==============================================================================

user.sgit.ai / the account

# The account model: door, master, vaults

You are already signed in, somewhere else: to Apple on a Mac, to Google in Chrome, to Microsoft on Windows, and that is where your passkeys live. The site does not need you to sign in to it. It asks the passkey store you already use for 32 bytes, computes from them the address and the key of a small door vault, finds the master's key inside, and the master holds everything else. There is no account database because there is no account, only vaults the user can open.

 The passkey store iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, Windows Hello, a hardware key. Syncs the passkey between devices. Learns nothing about the vault. [chosen long before]

 →

 The passkey, with PRF A gesture, a signature, and 32 bytes computed from a secret the authenticator keeps for this site. The same bytes on every device, through the same kind of path. [a lock, not an identity]

 →

 The door One file, at an address computed from the bytes: the master's key, encrypted under the door's read key, and a record of where the door came from. [one per path]

 →

 The master The keyring. The keys of the vaults below, by site and purpose; read keys the user was given; the access key; the key pairs; the list of doors. [random, made once]

 →

 The vaults below The reader vault (activity, one file per device). The billing vault (proposed). A notes vault. Whatever an agent makes for the user. [the user's data]

## What each piece actually gives you

The pieces are easy to blur, so the passkey article separates them, and this table is its table.

 Piece | What it gives the page | What it does not give | 

 The account you are already signed in to (Apple, Google, Microsoft) | Nothing, directly. It syncs your passkey store between your devices, so the passkey you make on one is on the others. | Anything to the site: not your name, not your email, not that you have an account. | 

 A passkey for this site | A gesture (touch, face, PIN), a signature, and with PRF, 32 bytes computed from a secret the authenticator keeps for this site and this passkey. | The bytes to anyone but the page on this site that asked, after the gesture; and not, in 2026, the same bytes by every path. | 

 The path | How the passkey was reached: the provider on this device, a phone over the hybrid link, a hardware key. | A guarantee that two paths compute the same bytes. | 

 The passkey store | Where the passkey lives, and whether it travels. | Anything about what the bytes are for. | 

 sgit | Vault keys made in the client (a 24-character passphrase and an 8-character vault id), read and write keys derived from them, ciphertext on the server, files that can be deleted, vaults that can be destroyed. | A way to find a vault you have no key for; a way to reuse a destroyed id. | 

 The access key | The right to create vaults and write to them on the vault server. The thing people will buy. | Any way to read a vault. | 

One clarification that matters. “The Google passkey” is a passkey for this site, registered by this page under this site's name, which your store keeps and syncs. It is not the passkey you use to sign in to Google, and a website cannot get PRF bytes from that one. The site learns a credential id, a public key and, after your gesture, 32 bytes. Not your email, not your name, not which account syncs it.

## The derivation

From the bytes to a door, as the newsroom's lab runs it with the relying party newsroom.sgit.ai, and as this site's lab runs it with user.sgit.ai. Only the constant differs.

 - The PRF input is a fixed, public value: SHA-256("user.sgit.ai/door/v1"). An input is not a secret; only the authenticator can turn it into the 32 bytes.

 - The door seed is HKDF-SHA256(ikm = PRF bytes, salt = SHA-256("user.sgit.ai"), info = "sgit/door/v1").

 - The door's passphrase and vault id are two more HKDF outputs from the seed. The passphrase is the hex of 32 bytes, keeping all 256 bits. The vault id is 8 characters of [a-z0-9] drawn with rejection sampling, so no character is favoured. The id is the door's address.

 - The door vault key is the sgit vault key made of those two, and from there sgit's own derivation gives the read and write keys exactly as the command line does: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations, once for each. That is the cost of the design: door, master and reading vault need up to six derivations, about 105 ms each in headless Chromium on a four-core machine, several times slower on a phone, so a cold unlock can spend two to four seconds deriving keys before it fetches anything.

 - The recovery door is the same, with the recovery code in place of the PRF bytes: 26 characters of base32, 128 bits, made by the page and shown once.

 - Collisions are not a practical worry with 368 possible ids, but the page checks: a derived address that already holds something it cannot open is skipped, with a counter in the HKDF info.

The browser and the command line agree byte for byte: the newsroom publishes test vectors computed with sgit's own Python, and this site's lab runs the same derivation through its own copy of the code and compares every value when the page opens.

## What is in each vault

 Vault | Holds | Status | 

 A door | One file. The master vault's key, encrypted under the door's read key, and a small record: the kind of door (a passkey, or the recovery code), the provider as the browser named it, the path (platform or cross-platform), the credential id, which is public, a device label the reader typed, and the date. | runs | 

 The master | The keyring. The keys of the vaults below it, by site and purpose. Read keys the user has been given. The access key, pasted once on the first device. The key pairs for this site, a signing pair and an encryption pair, each with a label, a purpose, a date and a status. The list of doors, each with its own vault key, so that from any open door the page can read, rewrite or delete every other door. Since newsroom v0.12.58 also inbox.json, which remembers where a connected browser's batches are filed. | runs keys; designed key pairs | 

 The reader vault | One file per device, rewritten whole on each sync: reads, top-ups, personas, notes, the wire stories seen. activity/account.json written once, with the one starting credit. activity/aliases.json for merged devices. An inbox lane any browser with a link can write to and none can read. A read-only link to the shared viewer vault, so the vault opens as an app in SG/Vault. | runs | 

 The billing vault | One per user. Activity and claims, signed by the user. Validations, signed by the admin. Its first commit pinned, so every later commit can be checked to descend from it and to be signed by a known key. | proposed | 

 The recovery door | The same as a door, with the recovery code as its ikm. The one secret a person ever types, and only on a device where no door opens. | runs | 

### The data, as the reader vault lays it out today

activity/
 account.json written once: { v, start, symbol, created, created_by }
 aliases.json merged device ids, each mapped to the device it went into
 devices/
 nr-3f9a1c2b.json one per device, rewritten whole on each sync
 nr-77e0b4d1.json

a device file:
{ "v": 1,
 "device": { "id", "label", "agent", "first_sync", "last_sync", "syncs" },
 "created": "the local account's creation time",
 "reads": [ { id, at, path, title, kind, topics, price, depth, cost, persona, rating?, declined?, device } ],
 "topups": [ { ref, at, credit, source, device } ],
 "personas": [ { id, preset?, name, created, on[], off[], device } ],
 "notes": [ { id, at, kind, path, title, text, quote, sent?, device } ],
 "wire": { "seen": { "<story id>": { at } } },
 "active": "me" }

Every record is the meter's own, unchanged, plus the device that originated it. A record has exactly one author for ever: the device, and a device is a bucket the reader names. The totals are recomputed every time they are shown:

 Figure | From the records | 

 reads | the number of distinct read ids across every device | 

 spent | the sum of cost over those reads (a declined read's cost is 0) | 

 declined | the sum of declined.refunded | 

 credit | the sum of credit over top-ups, one per payment reference | 

 balance | start + credit − spent | 

## A door per path

The unit of the design is the path, not the passkey, because of a test. The same Google Password Manager passkey gave the same bytes in Chrome on a Mac and in Safari on an iPhone through the provider on each device, and a different set of bytes, consistently, when an iPad or that same Mac reached the phone by QR code. Apple's forums report the same for iCloud Keychain since late 2024.

 Run | Client | How the passkey answered | Bytes | 

 1 | Chrome on a Mac | Google Password Manager on the Mac, Touch ID | A | 

 2 | Safari on an iPhone | Google Password Manager on the phone, Face ID | A | 

 3 | Safari on an iPad | A QR code, scanned by the iPhone; the phone's provider answered | B | 

 4 | Chrome on the same Mac, “use a phone, tablet or security key” | A QR code, scanned by the same iPhone | B | 

So whatever produced a distinct set of bytes gets a distinct door, and every door points at the same master and says where it came from. If a provider's fix moves a path's bytes, that path finds no door, says so, and the reader adds one. The design never has to guess which output was correct. It only has to keep every door replaceable. That is also why the master's key is random and sits behind a door rather than being derived from the bytes directly: derived directly, a path with other bytes would derive another master, and nothing could join the two.

## Keys and parties

Every key in the design, who holds it, and what it can and cannot do. The last four rows are the billing proposal's; the rest run today.

 Key | Held by | Can | Cannot | 

 The PRF bytes | Only the page, in memory, after the gesture | Derive a door's address and key | Be read by the store, the site operator or the vault server | 

 A door's vault key | Nowhere; recomputed on each unlock | Open one door | Open anything else | 

 The master's key | Every door, encrypted; the page's memory while unlocked | Open the keyring | Be derived from the passkey | 

 A vault key (reader, billing, notes) | The master | Read and write that vault | Be shared partly; there is no partly-public vault key | 

 A read key | Whoever was given it; a page, printed | Clone and decrypt one vault | Write to it, or be turned into write access | 

 The access key | The master, pasted once on the first device | Create vaults and write to the upload server | Read any vault | 

 An append token | The sender of a message or a connected browser | Write to one lane | List, fetch or read anything | 

 An enum key | The vault's owner | List, fetch and mark messages in a lane | Write | 

 A signing pair and an encryption pair | The master; made at random, never derived from the passkey | Sign activity and claims; receive secrets encrypted to the public half | Change when a lock changes | 

 The admin key | The admin's device; made there, never exported | Sign a validation of credit | Invent activity the user did not sign | 

 The upload server's key | The upload server | Check a key against the register and read a signed credit | Compute a balance; it keeps no database | 

 The credits API's key | The credits API | Serve a cached, signed credit with an end date | Validate anything itself | 

### The four parties

 Party | Writes | Reads | Can be offline | 

 The user | Their own activity, and claims (“I paid”), signed with their key | Everything in their own vaults | Yes; local storage stays primary | 

 The admin vault | Licensing and validation records, signed with the admin key | Usage from the users' vaults, close to anonymised; payments from Stripe | Yes, for hours; it catches up | 

 The upload server | Ciphertext it is given; a count of what it serves | A cached, signed credit, and the key register | No; it is the one server left | 

 The credits API | Nothing | The latest signed validation per billing vault | Briefly; the record carries valid_until | 

## Security, said plainly

 - What each party sees. The vault server: ciphertext, sizes, times and ids that look random. Your platform account: that a passkey exists for this site, under the name you gave it. The provider that answers a PRF request: the request, and that it answered. Only this page, in your browser, after your gesture, holds the PRF bytes and the keys.

 - Whoever can use the passkey by a path that has a door can reach everything below the master. That is exactly the passkey's protection, the biometric, the device and the store, and nothing in this stack adds to it or weakens it. A second passkey for an admin master is how the reach is split.

 - A path's bytes are a key a provider lends. Two paths can compute different bytes from one credential, and a provider's fix could change either. The door layer makes that survivable: no door is the only way in.

 - The origin loads no third-party scripts, on any page. Storage is per origin. Enforced by the build.

 - The relying party ID is a trust boundary. This site registers passkeys for user.sgit.ai exactly.

 - Passkeys cannot be phished across sites. They are bound to the site's name; a look-alike domain gets nothing.

 - Losing everything is final. Every door's passkey and the recovery code gone means no one can open the vaults. That is the property that makes the design worth having, and the first run says so before it shows the code.

 - Availability is not secrecy. The vault server could delete or roll back ciphertext. It cannot read it. The local copy covers the first; nothing is needed for the second.

 - Agents do not have passkeys. An agent that should read part of a user's data gets a read key for one vault, given by the user from the master, never the master itself.

 - Activity reported by the browser is on trust where the cost to us is small. What costs real money, storage and transfer, is counted at the server where it happens.

## Where PRF works today

As of October 2026, from vendor documentation, published tests and the newsroom's own. The page checks prf.enabled when it creates the passkey, and never guesses.

 Passkey provider | PRF | What the reader gets | 

 Google Password Manager (Chrome, Edge, Samsung Internet; Android) | Yes, by default; desktop Chrome from version 136 | The same account everywhere, by the platform path | 

 iCloud Keychain (Safari 18, macOS 15) | Yes; tested on a Mac, an iPad and an iPhone, in Safari and Chrome | The same account on every Apple device, by the platform path | 

 Windows Hello | Yes, since the February 2026 update to Windows 11 | This PC, or every PC on the account if synced | 

 Firefox | Yes, on macOS from version 139 and Windows from version 148 | As its store allows | 

 Hardware security keys | Yes through hmac-secret, but not with YubiKeys in Safari | No account anywhere; a few dozen passkeys per key | 

 Your phone, by QR (the hybrid flow) | Where the phone's store does, with bytes of its own | A door of its own, added once | 

 Chrome's own profile store | No, in 2026 tests | Signs, returns no bytes: no door can be derived; it can hold the recovery code | 

When PRF is off, the page offers a ladder, in this order: sign in to a store, so the passkey syncs from now on; use your phone by QR, with its own door; plug in a hardware key; or stay on this device, where the browser's own copy keeps working and the recovery code is the way back.

 ← The front page
 The workflows →


==============================================================================
== workflows/index.html
==============================================================================

user.sgit.ai / the workflows

# Ten client-side user workflows

User management on a site with no server of its own is not one feature. It is a set of things a person does, each of which their browser has to do entirely on its own, against a passkey store for the gesture and a vault server for ciphertext. These are the ten, as they run on newsroom.sgit.ai or as they are designed, on 21 Oct 2026. Each says what the user does, what the browser does, what leaves the browser, and where it stands.

The status chips. runs you can do it today, on the newsroom, as a beta with one reader. lab-proven a card in a lab did it once against a real vault server. designed written down in enough detail to build, not built. proposed an argument with its open questions listed. later named, with the ways it could go.

1
### Sign in where you already are

What the user does. Presses one button and makes the gesture their device already asks for: Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello, a hardware key's PIN. No email, no password, no OAuth. The first screen is the passkey, and one line says that it lives in the store you already use and goes where it goes.

What the browser does. Asks the store for the passkey for this site with the PRF extension and a fixed public input. Gets 32 bytes. Derives the door's address and key from them (the derivation), fetches the door's one file, decrypts the master's key, opens the master, and from it opens the reader vault. Reading needs no access key, so a device that can open a door can read before it can write; the access key comes out of the master, so it can write too. The keys of an unlocked session are kept in memory and, for the life of the tab, in session storage, so moving from page to page does not ask for the passkey each time: a choice for the beta, written down so it can be revisited.

What leaves the browser. A PRF request to the passkey store. Plain GETs of ciphertext to the vault server. Not a name, not an email, not a password, not the bytes.

runs The vault pane on every newsroom page, since v0.11.0; the Vault button beside the balance. On this origin, the lab does the gesture and the derivation and stops before any server.

2
### The first device: create the account

What the user does. Opens the pane, enables with the passkey, and is told no door here for this path yet. Pastes the access key, once, on this first device. Presses Create the account . Writes down the recovery code, shown once, after a sentence that says losing every passkey and the code is final.

What the browser does. Makes the master's key and the reader vault's key at random. Creates the door at its derived address, the master, the reader vault and the recovery door, with the access key. Puts the access key in the master, so a second device gets it by opening the master. Moves the reading account from this browser's local storage into the reader vault as the first device's file. From newsroom v0.12.1, an account made without an access key in its master asks for it once.

What leaves the browser. Encrypted commits, each one POST /batch to the vault server with the access key as a header, and a publish with compare-and-swap on the ref. The vault server stores ciphertext and hashes.

runs newsroom v0.11.0. The key pairs the brief asks for in the master (designed, step 5) are not made yet.

3
### Open, or connect

What the user does. Chooses one of two ways in, and names nothing first. Open your vault with the passkey (or the recovery code, once): this browser reads and writes. Connect with a link from a browser where the vault is already open, as a URL, text or a QR code: this browser only sends, into the vault's inbox lane, and never reads, not even what it sent. The second is for a browser that cannot reach the passkey: a web view an app opened, a browser signed in to nothing, an old iPad kept light for reading.

 | Open your vault | Connect with a link | 

 needs | the passkey, or the recovery code once | the link, which carries where to write and the key to encrypt to, nothing else | 

 reads the vault | yes | no, nothing | 

 writes | its own device file, one commit per update | one sealed message per send, into the inbox lane | 

 the meter shows | the whole account, once what the vault holds is brought in | this browser alone | 

What the browser does. Four states: nothing; connected (the link in local storage, Send to my vault on every page); open with the device unknown; open with the device known. Opening is the full membership; connecting is the push-only one, and the site is not personalised there. What matters in that browser is that the reads, the decisions and the notes are captured, because they are the reader's own intelligence and the reason they come back.

What leaves the browser. Open: as workflow 1, plus commits. Connect: one account-less POST per send to an append lane, encrypted to the vault's public key, with a response that is deliberately blind.

runs newsroom v0.12.58, open, or connect; the inbox lane since v0.12.26.

4
### Which device is this?

What the user does. After an explicit open, and only when there is a choice, answers one question: is this browser a device the vault already knows, or a new one? The chooser offers first the device whose name this browser used, or the one device on the same platform, and the button names the destination. Later, from the Vault tab, Change moves this browser into another device, and Merge ticks two or more devices and folds them into one with a name.

What the browser does. Choosing an existing device takes its id and label, and the merge that follows brings that device's records in as this browser's own. A new device needs no name. Two browsers may share a device, so every write is combine(prev, extract(local)) rather than an overwrite: every record of either, the one that knows more where both have it. A merge re-files each source into the target, keeps every record, removes the merged files from the current tree (every earlier version stays in the commits), and writes the merged ids to activity/aliases.json, so a browser still using one is filed under the merged device next time, and so is anything it sends. Nothing is dropped; a payment record is moved, never deleted.

What leaves the browser. Commits, as before. The device label is free text and only a hint; nothing is refused for a name.

runs The chooser in v0.12.58; merging, aliases and Change in v0.12.88, the vault, opened. Not built: splitting a merged device back out.

5
### Update the vault, bring them here

What the user does. Reads. Presses Update the vault when they want this device's activity in the vault; the Vault button counts what is only in this browser, and a strip above the tabs offers the press on any page. On another device, presses Bring them here , or has it done for them: after an explicit open the merge runs on its own, because the reader asked for the vault and the vault is the account.

What the browser does. Local storage stays primary, written in real time by the meter; the vault is a copy the reader keeps current. One file per device, rewritten whole on every sync, one commit. Two devices never write the same file, so there is nothing to merge at the file level and no conflict by construction; the compare-and-swap on publish still guards the ref. The other direction, inbound(), counts what a merge would add without writing, and shows it as Not yet here. On a page change the saved session opens the vault silently and nothing is merged: a reload under a reader who is reading is not acceptable. A Calls tab names and decrypts every call the pane made to the vault server, so the reader can see what left and what came back.

What leaves the browser. One commit per press. Nothing on a timer.

runs newsroom v0.11.0, v0.12.6, v0.12.58, v0.12.88; the design in the activity vault. Not built: automatic sync on a timer or on leaving a page; pruning local records the vault already holds.

6
### Read, and pay for what you read

What the user does. Reads. Starts with £5.00 of credit, is charged a few pence a page by how much of it they read, never less than a tenth of the page's price, and can go below zero without anything being blocked. Can pause all measuring, on every page, until they resume; reset a page to unread and have it refunded to the minimum; mark any section read or unread by hand; and say at the foot of a page that it was not worth it, in which case it is not charged. Tops up with a payment link when they want to.

What the browser does. Measures reading section by section: time on each section while the tab is in front and the reader active, against the section's words at 300 a minute, or text passing the reading line no faster than 450 words a minute. Keeps balance, history and receipts in local storage. Computes the totals from the records: reads, spent, declined, credit, balance = start + credit − spent. What was read also builds the reader's graph and their own front page.

What leaves the browser. Nothing, unless the reader chooses: a payment on Stripe's own page, a subscription, or a reading share. The reading itself is on trust: the reader can set the price of a page, edit their own balance, or start again in a private window. Every one of those changes a number only the cheater sees, so the gaps are accepted rather than closed with a server.

runs SG Meter v1.5.0 on every newsroom article, charging by what is read since v0.12.99 (17 October 2026); the controls in your reading, your controls.

7
### Top up: credit now, validated later

What the user does. Follows a £5 payment link to Stripe's page, pays, and comes back. The credit is there the moment they return, and they carry on. Nothing central sits in the path of their work.

What the browser does, today. The return page gives the credit; the payment reference makes the top-up unique across devices, because a merged top-up is also added to the device's list of credited references, so a return page opened again on another device cannot credit the same payment twice.

What the browser does, as proposed. The payment link carries a client_reference_id, the billing vault's id, never anything secret. On return the browser adds the credit straight away and appends a signed claim, “I paid”, to the billing vault. Later, hours later if need be, the admin's browser lists recent payments from Stripe with a restricted, read-only key that stays on the admin's machine, matches each claim to a payment, and commits a signed validation into the same vault. Credit is then in one of three states, and the product carries on in all three because on the client it costs us nothing:

 State | Meaning | 

 Not yet validated | The user paid, or says they did, and the admin side has not checked yet. Normal, and short-lived; a bank debit can take 2 to 14 days to confirm and simply stays here longer. | 

 Validated | The admin side matched it to a payment in Stripe, and signed it. | 

 Not valid | No matching payment. Unlikely; it means an attack, or a bug, and it shows up the next time the admin side runs. | 

What leaves the browser. Today: the payment, on Stripe's page. Proposed: the signed claim, as a commit to the billing vault.

runs The payment link, live since 11 October 2026. proposed The claim, the validation and the three states: the user keeps the meter.

8
### A new path, a lost device

What the user does. On a device whose path has no door (a new tablet whose only route is a QR code to the phone, or a path whose bytes a provider's fix has moved), reads no door here for this path yet, never an error, and takes one of two ways in: add the door from a device that is already open, or type the recovery code. In the first week, on a Mac with Chrome where both paths run, adds the QR path as a door in two gestures: open the door you have, then ask for the bytes by the other path. On losing a device, deletes its door from any open one.

What the browser does. Adding a door moves no key through a person: the page is unlocked, so the master's key is in memory; it derives the new door from the other path's bytes, encrypts the master's key under the new door's read key, writes the door's one file with the access key, and adds the door to the master's list. The provider that answered sees a PRF request and returns bytes; it never sees a key. A door is retired by deleting its one file, never by destroying its address, because the address is derived from the passkey and the path and would be lost for ever. Deleting a lost device's door stops that path from finding the master from the next unlock on; it does not undo a copy of the master's key the device may have had in memory, so the full answer is to rotate the master's key and rewrite the doors that are kept.

What leaves the browser. One door file, written. One door file, deleted.

lab-proven One door created at its derived address, opened again as a new device would, and deleted, on a real vault server; the pane's Add this device with the code runs. designed Adding a door by the other path while unlocked (the brief's step 6); rotating the master's key.

9
### Across sites

What the user does, today. Nothing yet. The master is bound to the newsroom: its passkey is registered for newsroom.sgit.ai exactly, and a passkey for sgit.ai is ruled out, because any *.sgit.ai site could ask it for bytes and every one would have to be as strict as the strictest.

What is designed. The master already lists keys by site and purpose, and the billing article's promise rests on it: “because the user's data lives in their vault, it travels with them across our sites: what they read, what they set, what they bought, their keys and their preferences.” Two ways to get there are named, for later. A key hub , in the manner of secrets.sgit.ai, holds the master and hands a site only the key to its own vault, after the user approves it in a pop-up, the way a wallet connects to a site. Or WebAuthn Related Origin Requests let one passkey work on a list of related sites, in Chrome and Safari today.

The question this site carries. Is user.sgit.ai the hub, the origin that holds the door and hands each sibling the key to its own vault? Or does each site keep its own relying party and the hub stays at secrets.sgit.ai? Both are consistent with the two articles; neither has been decided. It is N3 on the comms page, put to the project lead rather than answered for tidiness.

later Named in The passkey opens the vault, part two, and in what the user gets.

10
### Agents, messages and sessions

Give an agent a key. Agents do not have passkeys. An agent that should read part of a user's data gets a read key for one vault, given by the user from the master, never the master itself. An agent that should write gets its own private clone branch, and the work meets on a named branch a human reviews. runs as sgit's two-branch model; the handover from a master is designed.

Send a message. Every user now has a vault, every vault can have append lanes, and lanes plus PKI make a messenger: encrypted to the recipient's public key, signed by the sender, carried through a server that sees only ciphertext, size and time. The sender holds an append token that can write to one lane and nothing else; the owner holds the enum key that lists and fetches and cannot write. Messaging-FS is the proposed schema, one JSON file per conversation, next to Issues-FS and Email-FS. runs The reader vault's inbox lane (v0.12.26) and the newsroom's editor channel. proposed Deriving the lane address from the public key, one encoding, signing the whole envelope, the schema and the commands: Messaging-FS.

Hold a session. A temporary AWS session, one to twelve hours of credentials from the AWS access portal, pasted into a vault made for that session; the browser does the work with the normal AWS SDK for JavaScript, and what it finds, inventories, logs and costs, goes back into the vault, versioned and ready for graphs. The roles should be narrow, the sessions short, and the site's own code released the way the API sites are, each version a fixed, independent copy. proposed AWS from the vault; nothing built, and the name not decided.

What leaves the browser. A read key, handed to one agent for one vault. A sealed message, to a lane. AWS calls, from the browser, with credentials that live in the vault for the session and never in a page or a repository.

Three workflows that follow from the first nine: once the user holds the keys, every handover is a key given for one purpose, and every message is a signed file in a lane.

## What they have in common

 - Nothing is typed twice, and no key passes through a person except the access key once and the recovery code where no door opens.

 - Every step runs in the browser , against the passkey store for the gesture and the vault server for ciphertext.

 - Records, never totals. Balance, reads and credit are recomputed from the records every time they are shown.

 - The user chooses when to sync. One button; nothing commits on its own.

 - Soft enforcement. The way in is never a form; a name is a hint; nothing is refused for a label. What the client reports is on trust where the cost is small, and counted at the server where the cost is real.

 - An unknown address is not an error. It means a door is not there yet, and the page says so.

 ← The account model
 Billing →


==============================================================================
== billing/index.html
==============================================================================

user.sgit.ai / billing

# The user keeps the meter

A proposed design for user management, activity and billing on vaults, with one billing vault per user, two signed writers, and one light check at the server. It is the design in the article of the same name, 21 October 2026, set out here as the billing half of this site, with its status kept honest: nothing in it is built , the record formats are sketches, and the Stripe flow is untested.

A proposal. The pieces it builds on exist and are in use today: the meter, the append lanes, the versioning and the key register. The billing vault, the admin vault, the credits API and the upload server's check do not. Every open question is listed at the end, and the one about where this lives is on the comms page.

## In short

 - Billing is usually a server problem. A database, a balance every action updates, and races.

 - This proposal does it on the client. Each user has a billing vault; their browser keeps the meter.

 - Two writers, two keys. The user signs activity; the admin signs the validation of credit.

 - Credit now, validated later. The user carries on straight away; the admin side catches up.

 - Stripe is reconciled from the admin's browser. Payments are read, matched and validated.

 - One server, one light check. The upload server asks: is the key valid, and is there credit?

 - The user's data travels with them. Across every site, because it lives in their vault.

## The old problem

Every time billing has been built here, it has had the same shape. A server and a database. Every action a user takes updates something central, a balance, a usage count, and the moment two actions arrive at once there is a race on that balance. The usual way out is to append first and update later, write every event to a log and work out the balance from it, but then either every action goes through the thing that updates the balance, which becomes the bottleneck, or the update runs on a schedule, a cron job or a set of functions, which works, and is messy, and is one more thing to run, watch and pay for.

## What already exists

 Piece | Where it runs | 

 A meter in the reader's browser. Every reader starts with £5 of credit, each page draws a few pence by how much of it was read, the credit is kept in the browser, the balance can go below zero, and a £5 payment link tops it up. | newsroom.sgit.ai, live since 11 October 2026 | 

 Append lanes. A vault can have a lane that others write to and only its owner reads; a hundred writers on one lane have been measured. | The reader vault's inbox; the editor's channel | 

 Version control. Every change is a commit; two writers' changes can be seen, ordered and merged, which is exactly what a balance kept in a file was missing. | Every vault | 

 Keys. Every message, secret and handover starts with a signature, and the public keys live in a register anyone can check. | pki.sgit.ai | 

## The idea

The insight that makes it work is a simple one. A user very rarely runs several clients at the same time. The race that hurts a central server, many writers on one balance, mostly does not exist for one person's own activity. And for the cases where it does, two tabs, or a laptop and a phone, the vault's version control already does the merging. So each user has a vault that tracks their own activity. Their browser collects what they do, at intervals, and appends it there. That is the newsroom's meter, use first then buy or top up, with the record kept in a vault rather than only in one browser, so it can be backed up, synced, checked and billed.

 The user's browser Meters its own use. Appends activity. Adds credit when it pays. [signs with the user's key]

 →

 The billing vault, one per user Activity and claims, signed by the user. Validations, signed by the admin. First commit pinned. [two writers]

 →

 The admin vault In the admin's browser. Reads usage. Reads payments from Stripe. Commits validations back. [signs with the admin key]

 →

 The credits API A simple read of the latest signed validation, cached, with an end date. [its own key]

 →

 The upload server Key valid? Credit left? Then it does the work, and counts what it serves. [the one server left]

## Two writers, two keys

One billing vault per user, which two parties can write to, and each signs only what it is responsible for.

 - The user writes activity. Their browser commits what they used, signed with the user's key. That record belongs to them: they can read it, keep it and take it elsewhere.

 - The admin validates credit. When the user comes back from paying, their browser adds the credit straight away, with a signed claim. Later, the admin side checks that claim against Stripe and commits a validation into the same vault, signed with the admin key. Anyone can verify it against the admin's public key, and nobody else, the user included, can write a validation that verifies.

A validation record could be as small as this. The field names are a sketch, not a format:

{
 "billing_vault": "the vault's id",
 "claims": [
 { "claim": "the user's claim commit", "stripe_event": "the event's id",
 "pence": 500, "status": "validated" }
 ],
 "validated_balance_pence": 4210,
 "covers_activity_to": "the last activity commit counted",
 "as_of": "2026-10-21T10:00:00Z",
 "valid_until": "2026-10-28T10:00:00Z",
 "signed_by": "the admin key's fingerprint",
 "signature": "over everything above"
}

The user can add credit their browser believes in, but cannot make it validated, and the admin cannot invent activity the user did not sign.

## The admin vault, and Stripe

The other half is a central admin vault, which the admin controls. Usage data flows into it from the users' vaults, close to anonymised but tied to the user so it can be billed, and it is where payments are reconciled with Stripe, from the admin's browser. Stripe's own constraints, from its documentation read on 21 October 2026, shape how:

 - Webhooks need a server. Registered endpoints must be publicly accessible HTTPS URLs, signed with a shared secret, not a public key. That does not fit a design with no server to receive them.

 - So the admin side reads instead. Stripe's API lists events going back up to 30 days, so the admin's browser pulls recent payments when it runs, rather than waiting for a push.

 - The key that reads Stripe stays on the admin's machine. Only publishable keys are safe outside a backend; here the admin's browser plays the backend, with a restricted key that can only read.

 - A payment can say which vault it is for. A payment link carries a client_reference_id, returned with the completed payment. It should be the billing vault's id, never anything secret.

So the flow is: the user is sent to Stripe with a payment link tagged with their billing vault; Stripe sends them back to a page that gives them the credit, and their browser adds it straight away and appends a signed claim; later, the admin's browser lists recent payments, matches each claim to a payment, and commits a signed validation. Two-way sync between two vaults, with each side writing only its own records.

User's browser -> Stripe pay with a payment link, tagged with the billing vault
Stripe -> User's browser back to a page that gives the credit
User's browser -> Billing vault add the credit now, with a signed claim
 (the user carries on straight away)
Admin's browser -> Stripe later: list recent payments, with a read-only key
Admin's browser -> Billing vault match the claim to the payment
Admin's browser -> Billing vault commit a signed validation, or "not accepted"
Upload server -> Billing vault read the signed validation, cached
Upload server -> Upload server check the signature and the balance

## Credit now, validated later

The user should be able to use what they paid for straight away, so the credit goes into their browser the moment they come back from Stripe. The check comes afterwards, as a layer on top. The admin side does not need to be online when the user pays; it can catch up hours later, and when it does it adds a note to the user's vault, signed as the commercial authority: validated, or not accepted. Stripe's own guidance fits this order: fulfilment cannot rely on the checkout landing page, because customers are not guaranteed to visit it; the admin side reads Stripe directly, so a payment whose user never came back is still credited.

 State | Meaning | Who can produce it | 

 Credit not yet validated | The user paid, or says they did; the admin side has not checked. Normal, short-lived. | The user | 

 Credit validated | Matched to a payment in Stripe, and signed. | Only the admin key | 

 Credit not valid | No matching payment. An attack, or a bug. | Only the admin key | 

## Who is this defending against?

The party that could cheat is the user, by gaming the client: adding credit they did not pay for, or leaving out activity. In the short term that is unlikely, and it is easy to detect: every claim has to match a payment in Stripe, every commit is signed, and a claim with no payment behind it shows up as not valid the next time the admin side runs. So the design does not try to make cheating impossible on the client. It makes it visible, and puts the hard check where a mistake would cost money: at the server.

## A vault shared by two parties

There is a more general idea underneath. The billing vault is shared by an untrusted party, the user, and a trusted one, the admin. Once the vault exists, its first commit is pinned. From then on every later commit can be checked for consistency against it: that it descends from that first commit, and that it is signed by a key we know. That gives a two-way channel between the two parties, through the vault, where it is always known who did what. Billing is the first use; the same pattern fits any place where a user and a service need a shared record both can trust.

## The one server left

Most of the network's sites already run with no server of their own. The one that remains is the sgit upload server, which stores vaults, and it is also where usage costs money, in storage and transfer. So that is where the check belongs, and it stays light:

 - Is the key valid? A PKI check, against the register.

 - Is there credit? A read of the user's latest signed validation record, verified against the admin's public key.

The upload server does not compute a balance or keep a database of its own. It reads a cached, signed value through a small credits API with its own simple definition. A cached value can be slightly out of date, so the record carries valid_until, and the upload server can also count what it serves, so the units that cost real money are measured where they happen, not reported by the client. Today the access key gates use of the upload server but does not meter it; vault creation, for example, is not tracked per user. That is the gap this design fills.

## What the user gets

This is not only a billing design. Once a user is logged in, their data lives in their vault, and it travels with them across all of the network's sites: what they read, what they set, what they bought, their keys and their preferences. A logged-in user gets a better experience on every site, without each site keeping a copy of them on a server. How the account travels is workflow 9, and it is not decided.

## What it trusts, and what it does not

 Claim | Trusted? | Why | 

 Activity reported by the browser | on trust | As the newsroom's meter, where the reader can set the price of a page. Fine where the cost is small. | 

 Storage and transfer | counted | Measured at the server where they happen. | 

 Validated credit | cannot be forged | It needs the admin's signature. Unvalidated credit could be, and would show up as not valid. | 

 A cached credit record | a little stale | So it carries an end date. | 

 The admin key | matters most | Made on the device, never exported. | 

## Open questions

 - Where does it live? user.sgit.ai and api.user.sgit.ai, or billing.sgit.ai and api.billing.sgit.ai, so others can use it easily. Answered for this site on 21 October 2026: it is user.sgit.ai (N1). Whether billing also gets a site of its own, for others to use, is still open.

 - Should the upload server accept unvalidated credit? Where usage costs real money, it may want only validated credit, or a small amount on top.

 - Who creates the first vault? Maybe the service creates a user's first vault for them, when they first log in. The design assumes it already exists; the account model's first-device flow makes it with the access key the user pasted.

 - How does login work? A PKI handshake, as everything now does. The account model answers the first half: the passkey, the door, the master, the key pairs. The handshake with a site is the second.

 - How anonymous is the usage? The admin vault needs enough to bill, and should get no more.

 - How often does the browser sync? Often enough to bill, not so often it slows the user down. The activity vault's answer today is: when the reader presses the button.

 - How are refunds and disputes written? Probably as signed validation records too, with their own status.

## The versioned API sites

Whatever the API site is called, it would follow the rule the network's other API sites already use, written down on api.send.sgit.ai: every release is a complete, independent copy at its own versioned path, never edited after it is published, with a manifest of hashes. A site pins the version it uses, so a change to the API is a new version, not an edit to an old one. The same rule is asked of any site whose code holds a session for the user.

## What this does not claim

 - Nothing here is built. Neither the billing vault, the admin vault, the credits API nor the upload server's check exists.

 - The record formats are sketches. The field names will change.

 - The Stripe flow is not tested. Its constraints are from Stripe's documentation, read on 21 October 2026.

 - Client-reported activity is not proof. The design says where it is trusted and where it is counted.

 - The pieces it builds on exist. The meter, the append lanes, the versioning and the key register are in use today.

 ← The workflows
 The lab →


==============================================================================
== lab/index.html
==============================================================================

user.sgit.ai / the lab

# The lab: passkey to door, on this origin

The first workflow, sign in where you already are, as far as it can go without a server: a passkey for user.sgit.ai with the PRF extension, the 32 bytes, the door's address and sgit's keys derived from them, a recovery code, and the newsroom's test vectors run through this site's own copy of the derivation. Every card says what it did in the log at the foot.

This page writes nothing to any server. It talks to your passkey store for the gesture and to nothing else: no vault is created, no door is looked for, no byte of yours leaves this page. The only lasting effect is a passkey in your store, named as you choose, which you can delete there. The code is assets/door.js, vendored from the newsroom's with the relying party made a parameter, and assets/lab.js. No script on this origin comes from anywhere else.

### 1 · This browser

What the page can know before it asks for anything. Whether PRF works cannot be known until a passkey is made: the store says then, and the page never guesses.

Check again

### 2 · Make a passkey for this site

A discoverable credential for user.sgit.ai exactly, user verification required, with the PRF extension asked for, under a user handle this page chooses at random and a display name for the role. Your store may offer a choice of where to keep it: iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, a phone by QR, a hardware key. Where it lives decides where the account goes.

Make the passkey

### 3 · Get the bytes

One gesture. The page asks the store for the passkey for this site with the fixed public input SHA-256("user.sgit.ai/door/v1"), and the authenticator returns 32 bytes only it can compute. The card shows a fingerprint of them and the path the browser reports. The same passkey gives the same bytes on every device it syncs to, through the same kind of path; a phone over QR can give different bytes, and then the design gives that path a door of its own.

Get the bytes

### 4 · Derive the door

HKDF from the bytes to a seed, a 256-bit passphrase and an 8-character address; then sgit's own PBKDF2 at 600,000 iterations, once for the read key and once for the write key, the cost the design pays on every cold unlock. The address is where this passkey's door would be. Nothing is fetched: the lab does not ask the vault server whether a door exists there.

Derive the door

### 5 · A recovery code

128 bits as 26 characters of base32, shown in groups of four to be written down, long enough to need no password stretching. It is the ikm of a second door, the one way in on a device where no door opens yet, and the one secret a person ever types.

Make a code

Derive its door

### 6 · The test vectors, against sgit's Python

The newsroom publishes a fake PRF output and everything derived from it, computed in Python with sgit's own Vault__Crypto, for its relying party newsroom.sgit.ai. This site's copy of the derivation runs the same input with that relying party and compares seven values. It runs when the page opens.

Run again

### Forget

Clears the bytes, the door and the keys from this page's memory and the remembered label from this browser. The passkey stays in your store; a site cannot delete a passkey, only you can.

Forget on this device

## The log

## What this lab does not do

 - It makes no vault. The newsroom's lab goes further: with an access key kept in memory it makes real sgit vaults through the vault library vendored there, a door at its derived address, a master and a reader vault. This site has not vendored the library yet; that is T1 on the comms page, and when it is done the rule stays: pinned at a known commit, never edited, served from this origin.

 - It does not look for a door. A derived address with nothing at it would mean no door here for this path yet, never an error; the lab stops before the question.

 - It makes no key pairs. The identity the brief asks for, a signing pair and an encryption pair made at random and stored in the master, is designed and not built anywhere yet.

 - It is not tested by a virtual authenticator yet. The newsroom's pane is driven in Chromium with a virtual authenticator standing in for a synced passkey; this lab's derivation is checked by a Node test against the same vectors, and the gesture itself only by a person. T2.

 - It says nothing about which path is right. When two paths give different bytes, both need the credential's secret to check against the specification. The lab can say that each path was deterministic and that the two disagreed, and the design gives each a door.

 What this site ships →

user.sgit.ai / what this site ships

# What this site ships

What this site asserts, against what can be opened today, as of 21 Oct 2026. If this page and any other page on the site disagree, this page wins. Every row names where its evidence is.

## Runs today, on newsroom.sgit.ai

A beta with one reader, as the newsroom's own notes call it. You can do each of these on any newsroom page with the Vault button beside the balance.

 What | Since | Evidence | 

 Enable with a passkey; a door derived from the PRF bytes; a master; a reader vault; a recovery code as a second door | v0.11.0, 12 Oct 2026 | The activity vault | 

 One file per device, rewritten whole; totals recomputed from the records; Update the vault; Bring them here | v0.11.0; v0.12.6 | Same note; assets/vault-pane/sync.js on the newsroom, checked by admin/build/test_sync.mjs | 

 An inbox lane on the reader vault any browser with a link can write to and none can read | v0.12.26, 13 Oct | The note send to my vault from any browser | 

 Two ways in, open or connect; which device is this, asked after the open; what the vault holds merged in on an explicit open | v0.12.58, 13 Oct | Open, or connect | 

 Merging devices with aliases; a Calls tab that names and decrypts every call; a browse page; a shared viewer vault linked read-only into every reader vault | v0.12.88, 16 Oct | The vault, opened | 

 The reading meter, charged by what is read, with pause, reset and read/unread by hand; a balance that can go below zero | SG Meter v1.5.0, 17 Oct; v0.12.110, 18 Oct | Your reading, your controls | 

 A £5 payment link, credited on return, unique across devices by payment reference | 11 Oct | The account page | 

 The passkey lab: a passkey with PRF, the bytes with the path shown, the derivation, the recovery code, test vectors against sgit's Python, and real vaults made and opened in the browser with the vendored library | 11 and 12 Oct | The passkey lab | 

## Lab-proven, once

 - A door created at its derived address on a real vault server, opened again the way a new device would, and its file deleted. The newsroom's lab, 11 and 12 October, with one Google Password Manager passkey and one iCloud Keychain passkey, across a Mac, an iPad and an iPhone.

 - The derivation agrees with sgit's Python byte for byte , from a fixed test vector and from live bytes. This site's lab runs the same vectors through its own copy of the code, and a Node test does the same before a release.

 - The same passkey gave different bytes by the QR path than by the platform path, consistently. That finding is why the design has a door per path.

## Designed, not built

 - Key pairs in the master: a signing pair and an encryption pair, made at random on the first device, with the public halves published where the share page and the subscribe lane need them.

 - Adding a door by the other path while unlocked, with no key typed, offered in the first week as add your phone by QR.

 - Retiring a device and rotating the master's key; retiring a master in the order the article gives.

 - Several passkeys for several roles, as several masters, chosen in the provider's own picker.

 - Automatic sync on a timer or on leaving a page, as a setting; pruning local records the vault already holds.

 - The handover of a read key from a master to an agent, for one vault.

## Proposed, with open questions

 - One billing vault per user, two signed writers, credit now and validated later, Stripe reconciled from the admin's browser, a credits API and one light check at the upload server. 21 October 2026. Nothing built; the Stripe flow untested.

 - Messaging-FS: a messenger between vaults on append lanes and PKI. The transport exists; the schema and the commands do not.

 - AWS from the vault: a temporary AWS session kept in a vault for one session, the browser doing the work. Nothing built; the name not decided.

 - One account across sites: a key hub, or Related Origin Requests. Later.

## What this site itself does

 Claim | True? | How to check | 

 Publishes the client-side user workflows and the billing design, with every claim sourced to a dated article or note | yes | The sources | 

 Runs a lab that makes a passkey for user.sgit.ai, gets PRF bytes and derives a door's address, on this origin | yes | The lab; press the cards | 

 Writes nothing to any server, holds no account, keeps no user data | yes | View source; the lab's log; there is no fetch to any host but this one and the passkey store | 

 Loads no third-party script on any page | yes, enforced | The gate fails the build otherwise | 

 Has vendored the vault library and can make a vault in the browser | no, not yet | T1 | 

 Is registered in the sgit.ai network directory | no, not yet | T6; the Cartographer's prompt on sgit.ai | 

 Is served at user.sgit.ai, the name the billing article proposed | yes, from v0.1.1 | N1; the CNAME file |

 Three surfaces: which one are you building for? | This is a site page, outside every vault host: indexed, linkable, readable with no key. On this surface the site is the host and must distrust the vault. |

== network/index.html
==============================================================================

user.sgit.ai / the network

# The network

This site is one of a family of focused sites under sgit.ai, each pursuing one question further than a section of the parent could, each with its own version history and repository, and each linking rather than duplicating. This site owns the client-side user: the account with no server, the workflows a user runs in their browser, and the billing that follows. It borrows everything else.

## Who owns what

 Site | Owns | How this site uses it | 

 sgit.ai | The parent project: the vault layer, the CLI, the platform documentation, the three surfaces, the guidance for site pages. | The substrate every workflow runs on, and the guidance this site was built to. | 

 newsroom.sgit.ai | Pay for what you read; the vault pane; the passkey lab; the meter. | Where every workflow marked runs actually runs. This site describes; the newsroom does. | 

 pki.sgit.ai | A key registry for agents and people, designed from the 2019 keyserver failure. | The register the upload server checks a key against; where the admin's and the user's public keys would be published. | 

 secrets.sgit.ai | Moving a secret from A to B on public keys only; a vault for the private key; the keyring design. | One of the two ways named for one account across sites: a key hub that holds the master and hands a site only the key to its own vault. | 

 subscriptions.sgit.ai | A subscription is a discount for regular use, not rent. | The commercial model a billing vault would meter against; and the repository this site's build tooling was copied from. | 

 llms.sgit.ai | Calling a language model from a vault app with no API key. | The pattern for what an agent gets from a user: a key for one purpose, never the master. | 

 nhi.sgit.ai | Identity for agents you run and agents you rent. | Why agents do not have passkeys, and get read keys instead. | 

 api.send.sgit.ai | The API behind the vault server, and the rule of independent releases. | The rule any api.user.sgit.ai would follow: every release a complete, independent copy at its own versioned path. | 

 coding.sgit.ai | How the code across the family is written. | Followed by this site's build tooling and the lab's code. | 

## Where this site sits

The billing article left the question open: user.sgit.ai with api.user.sgit.ai, or billing.sgit.ai with api.billing.sgit.ai so that others can use it easily. This site is user.sgit.ai, the first of the two, chosen on 21 October 2026 (N1 on the comms page); api.user.sgit.ai is the name its client code would take. A billing part that stands on its own at billing.sgit.ai stays an option. It is not yet in the network directory on sgit.ai; adding it is the Cartographer's prompt there, and T6 here.

## What being part of a network costs

Every entry above is a link this site depends on and does not control. A sibling that has not shipped a page this site references is a fact about the network's build order, not a defect here, and it is checked rather than assumed: admin/build/check_siblings.py reports on it as a tool run by hand before a release, never as a gate, because a sibling's outage should not turn this repository's build red for a reason nobody here can fix.

 # | Ask | Why it needs you | Status |

 N2 | Who creates the first vault, and with whose access key? The account model has the user paste an access key once; the billing article asks whether the service should make a user's first vault for them when they first log in. | It decides whether a new user needs anything from us before they have an account, which is the whole point of the design. | Open | 

 N3 | Is this site the key hub? Two ways across sites are named: a hub that holds the master and hands each site the key to its own vault after a pop-up, or Related Origin Requests. If user.sgit.ai is the hub, it is the strictest origin in the network and every sibling connects to it; if not, each site keeps its own relying party and the hub is secrets.sgit.ai. | A design choice with a security boundary in it. Both are consistent with the articles; neither is decided. | Open | 

 N4 | Should the upload server accept unvalidated credit? Where usage costs real money, it may want only validated credit, or a small amount on top. | A commercial call, from the article's own open questions. | Open |

 N6 | Which workflows should this site run itself , beyond the lab? Today it describes, and the newsroom does. Making a vault here needs the vendored library (T1) and an access key in memory; the relying party is now settled as user.sgit.ai. | Scope: a reference site, or the account's home. | Open |

## Published unresolved

Not tasks. Questions the site carries in the open rather than answering for tidiness:

 - Which side of the QR path owns the PRF mismatch. The lab can say each path was deterministic and the two disagreed; it cannot say which is right. The design does not need to know, and the report to Apple and Google is the newsroom's step 12.

 - Whether a cold unlock of two to four seconds of key stretching is acceptable on a phone , or whether the keys should stay in session storage for the tab, as the beta does.

 - Whether the consolidated view should show a page read on two devices once or twice. The meter's rule today is once per session per device; the newsroom's experiment 2.

 - How often the browser should sync for billing , once the per-sync cost is known from the newsroom's experiment 1.
